passage: At her cousin's christening lunch in Cebu, Rosa counted the questions. Tita Lorna asked when she'd bring someone home. Tito Ben asked whether the bank teller job had a pension. Her grandmother patted her hand and said, 'Before thirty, anak, or the good ones are gone.' Rosa smiled through all of it, then locked herself in the bathroom and did the maths: meet someone this year, date for two, marry at twenty-eight... It already felt too late. Her savings were small. Cousins her age had babies on their hips. She texted Tariq, her friend from work: 'Everyone here has a timeline for me and I'm failing all of them.' He wrote back, 'Whose timeline, though?' Rosa stared at that, washed her face, and went back out for cake, still counting.

qa.q: What did Rosa's grandmother tell her?
qa.a: 'Before thirty, anak, or the good ones are gone.'

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling when she did the maths in the bathroom?
qa.a: Panic that time was running out; every step of the imagined timeline made her feel she was already too late 😰

qa.q: What opening does Tariq's reply give Rosa at this stage?
qa.a: His question 'Whose timeline, though?' invites her to see the deadline as her family's clock rather than a rule, which could loosen the sense of failure.

qa.q: How might Rosa's grandmother see her own advice?
qa.a: She likely means it as loving protection drawn from her own era's expectations, without seeing how heavily it lands on Rosa.

grounding: Shows the fear of being behind as family questions set a deadline for marriage and money, making ordinary variation feel like failure.

passage: The box of kaju katli went from desk to desk at the bank branch, and Damini followed it, glowing, holding out her phone with the engagement photo. Tanvir took a piece and said the right things. Then Mr Rao, the branch manager, leaned over: 'Your turn next, Tanvir? You're what, twenty-five? My son was settled by then.' Everyone laughed. Tanvir laughed too. At lunch he checked his account balance twice, then opened the message from Ammi with three biodata photos. His whole mohalla seemed to move in one direction on a fixed calendar, and he was standing still. By evening his chest was tight. He stayed late reconciling ledgers, not because they needed it, but because at home Ammi would ask again, and he had no answer that sounded like enough.

qa.q: What did Mr Rao ask Tanvir?
qa.a: 'Your turn next, Tanvir? You're what, twenty-five?'

qa.q: Why did Tanvir stay late reconciling ledgers?
qa.a: He was avoiding Ammi's questions because he feared his life would not sound like enough by his community's calendar.

qa.q: What turning point could help Tanvir at this stage?
qa.a: He could name the pressure to someone he trusts and ask whether that fixed calendar is really his; a calm talk with Ammi about his own plans might ease the dread.

qa.q: What might Damini be experiencing as her news goes round the branch?
qa.a: Damini is excited and sharing her joy, probably unaware that the celebration adds weight to Tanvir's day.

grounding: Illustrates the fear of being behind at 25 when a workplace joke and a tight-knit community's marriage timeline make a normal pace feel like failure.

passage:
The engagement was in a rented hall in Aliganj, marigolds everywhere, and Indu's younger cousin Abhinav was beaming on the stage.

"Now it's your turn, Indu," said Chhoti Bua, patting her cheek. "Twenty-six already. After twenty-eight, the good boys are gone."

Indu smiled the smile she'd practised. Another aunt asked about her salary; a third asked why she'd moved to Gurgaon alone.

In the washroom she stared at her face under the tube light. She had a job she mostly liked. She'd paid off her scooter. Six months ago she'd felt fine. Now, counting on her fingers, she felt like she was already late for a train everyone else had boarded.

Abhinav found her by the snacks table. "Didi, ignore them. Mummy used to say this to me when I was twenty-two."

Indu laughed, but her hands were still cold.

qa.q: Where was the engagement held?
qa.a: The engagement was in a rented hall in Aliganj.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling in the washroom?
qa.a: She felt anxious and suddenly behind, as if time was running out, even though six months earlier she had felt fine about her life.

qa.q: How could someone support Indu at this stage?
qa.a: A trusted cousin or friend could remind her that the 'deadline' is the family's clock, not a real rule, and help her name what she wants on her own timeline.

qa.q: How does Abhinav see what is happening to Indu?
qa.a: Abhinav sees the aunties' pressure as unfair and familiar, and wants to reassure her, though he may not realise how deeply it has shaken her.

grounding: At a family engagement, a 26-year-old feels time running out as relatives' marriage deadlines make her normal path feel like failure.

passage:
"Kalyani didi, did you see Mausi's message on the family group?"

"The one with the biodata? Yes. Delete it."

"She's sent three this month. Three." Pooja sat on the edge of the bed. "And Ma keeps saying, 'By twenty-seven it gets difficult.'"

"You're twenty-five."

"Exactly! Two years. Everyone in our colony is married. Sunaina has a baby. Even Babloo got engaged, and he still can't fry an egg."

"So?"

"So what if they're right? What if I wait and there's nothing?" Pooja's voice cracked. "I'm doing well at work. I like my life. But every time someone asks, I feel like I'm failing an exam I didn't know I was taking."

Kalyani sat down beside her. "I got married at twenty-three because of that exam. Don't let the colony hold the clock for you."

Pooja leaned against her didi's shoulder and didn't answer for a while.

qa.q: What did Mausi keep sending?
qa.a: Mausi kept sending biodata, three this month.

qa.q: What is Pooja worried about?
qa.a: Pooja is afraid that if she waits there will be nothing, and she feels anxious, like she is failing an exam she didn't know she was taking.

qa.q: What could Pooja try next, with her didi's help?
qa.a: She could agree with Kalyani on a calm, honest answer for relatives, and talk about what she herself wants in a partner and timeline, separate from the colony's clock.

qa.q: What is it like for Kalyani to hear Pooja's fear?
qa.a: Kalyani seems protective and a little regretful, since Kalyani admits marrying at twenty-three under the same pressure and wants a different path for her sister.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young woman's fear of being behind, driven by a tight-knit community's marriage clock that makes normal timing feel like failure.

passage:
In our para in Kolkata, everyone knows everyone's news before breakfast. So I knew about Trisha's wedding date before she told me.

I'm Gargi, and I'm twenty-six, and until this spring I'd have said I was fine. Good job at the publishing house. A tiny flat I love. Then Trisha got married, and the next week the tea-stall uncle asked Ma if "Gargi's arrangement" was happening soon.

Now I do sums in my head all the time. If I meet someone this year, marry at twenty-eight, a child by thirty. Every morning the numbers feel tighter, like the walls of a lift.

I know it's not a real deadline. Plenty of people I admire married late or never. But knowing it and feeling it are two different streets. Last night Trisha called from her honeymoon, happy, and I was happy for her, and then I cried in the bathroom anyway.

qa.q: Where does Gargi work?
qa.a: Gargi works at the publishing house.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling after Trisha's call from the honeymoon?
qa.a: Gargi felt genuinely happy for Trisha but also anxious and sad, afraid of being left behind, which is why Gargi cried afterwards.

qa.q: What could Gargi try next to ease this pressure?
qa.a: Gargi could name the para's clock as the source of the sums and talk with a trusted friend, perhaps Trisha herself, about what Gargi wants rather than what the timeline says.

qa.q: How might Gargi's Ma be affected when neighbours ask about an arrangement?
qa.a: Ma may feel pressured and awkward in front of the neighbours, caught between the community's expectations and her own child's life.

grounding: In a close-knit neighbourhood, a 26-year-old feels time running out, as social clocks turn normal variation into a sense of failure.

passage:
Note from the counsellor, company wellbeing programme, second session with Mohit
Mohit arrived early and talked fast. His cousin Anirban, a year younger, got engaged last week, and at the function three aunties asked Mohit when his turn was. His mother has started sending him profiles every evening. He listed his "deadlines": married by 27, own flat by 28, manager by 30. He said, "I'm already late for all of them." When I asked who set those dates, he paused. "Everyone. It's just how it's done in our community." He tapped his foot through the whole session. He said he has not been sleeping well and checks his colleagues' profiles every night.
What I did next: I asked him to write down which of those goals he actually wants and when, separately from what others expect. We talked about how people in his own office are marrying and settling at very different ages. He will bring the list next week.

qa.q: What did Mohit say his deadline was for being married?
qa.a: He said married by 27.

qa.q: How does Mohit feel about his deadlines?
qa.a: Mohit feels anxious and afraid of failing, tapping his foot and losing sleep because he believes he is already late for all of them.

qa.q: What turning point did the counsellor offer?
qa.a: The counsellor asked Mohit to separate what he truly wants from what others expect, and pointed out that people settle at very different ages.

qa.q: How might Mohit's mother see the profiles she sends each evening?
qa.a: His mother probably sees them as caring help and a normal family duty, not realising they add to Mohit's fear of falling behind.

grounding: Shows a young adult feeling time running out under community pressure to marry, earn and settle by fixed deadlines, making normal variation feel like failure.
